title: Module 4: Pulsed Ultrasound Parameters and Timing

questions.stem: Period is:
options: The time occupied by one pulse
The time required for one cycle
The time from the start of one pulse to the start of the next
The number of pulses per second
questions.explanation: Period is the time for one cycle.

questions.stem: Pulse duration is:
options: The total time occupied by one transmitted pulse
questions.explanation: Pulse duration is the total time of one transmitted pulse.

questions.stem: Pulse repetition period (PRP) is measured from:
options: The end of one pulse to the start of the next
The start of one cycle to the start of the next cycle
The end of transmit time to the end of receive time
The start of one pulse to the start of the next pulse
questions.explanation: PRP runs from the start of one pulse to the start of the next.

questions.stem: Pulse repetition frequency (PRF) is:
options: The number of pulses transmitted per second
The number of cycles in a pulse
The time required for one pulse
The distance occupied by one pulse
questions.explanation: PRF is pulses transmitted per second.

questions.stem: PRP and PRF are:
questions.explanation: PRF = 1 ÷ PRP.

questions.stem: Which parameter describes the physical distance occupied by one pulse?
questions.explanation: Spatial pulse length is the distance occupied by one pulse.

questions.stem: Which parameters describe pulse-to-pulse timing rather than individual cycles?
questions.explanation: PRP and PRF describe pulse-to-pulse timing.

questions.stem: Listening time is the part of the PRP during which the system:
questions.explanation: Listening time is when echoes are received.

questions.stem: The PRP consists of:
questions.explanation: PRP = pulse duration + listening time.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes an individual cycle?
questions.explanation: Period describes one cycle.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pulse parameter?
questions.explanation: Spatial pulse length describes a whole pulse.

questions.stem: Duty factor represents:
options: The fraction of time the system is listening
The fraction of time the system is transmitting pulses
The number of cycles in a pulse
The distance occupied by a pulse
questions.explanation: Duty factor is the fraction of time spent transmitting.

questions.stem: The duty factor of continuous wave ultrasound is:
questions.explanation: Continuous wave transmits all the time, so DF = 1 (100%).

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes period from pulse duration?
options: Period measures a pulse; pulse duration measures a cycle
Both measure the time between pulse starts
Period measures one cycle; pulse duration measures the whole pulse
questions.explanation: Period is one cycle; pulse duration is the entire pulse.

questions.stem: A pulse has 3 cycles, each with a period of 0.5 µs. What is the pulse duration?
A pulse has 5 cycles, each with a period of 0.25 µs. What is the pulse duration?
A pulse has 2 cycles, each with a period of 0.4 µs. What is the pulse duration?
A 2 MHz transducer emits a pulse of 4 cycles. What is the pulse duration?
A 5 MHz transducer emits a pulse of 3 cycles. What is the pulse duration?
A 4 MHz transducer emits a pulse of 2 cycles. What is the pulse duration?
A 3 MHz transducer emits a pulse of 6 cycles. What is the pulse duration?
A 1 MHz transducer emits a pulse of 3 cycles. What is the pulse duration?
With the number of cycles per pulse constant, increasing frequency causes pulse duration to:
questions.explanation: Higher frequency means a shorter period, so a shorter pulse.

questions.stem: With frequency constant, increasing the number of cycles per pulse causes pulse duration to:
questions.explanation: More cycles lengthen the pulse.

questions.stem: With the number of cycles constant, halving the frequency causes pulse duration to:
questions.explanation: Halving frequency doubles the period, doubling pulse duration.

questions.stem: The number of cycles doubles while the period is halved. Pulse duration:
questions.explanation: Cycles × period stays the same.

questions.stem: Which change decreases pulse duration when the number of cycles is constant?
questions.explanation: Higher frequency shortens the period and the pulse.

questions.stem: Which unit is appropriate for pulse duration?
questions.explanation: Pulse duration is a time (µs).

questions.stem: A pulse has 3 cycles and a wavelength of 0.5 mm. What is the spatial pulse length?
A pulse has 4 cycles and a wavelength of 0.3 mm. What is the spatial pulse length?
A pulse has 2 cycles and a wavelength of 0.77 mm. What is the spatial pulse length?
A 1 MHz pulse of 3 cycles travels in soft tissue (c = 1540 m/s). What is the spatial pulse length?
A 5 MHz pulse of 2 cycles travels in soft tissue (c = 1540 m/s). What is the spatial pulse length?
A pulse of 4 cycles has a spatial pulse length of 6 mm. What is the wavelength?
questions.explanation: λ = SPL ÷ cycles = 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 mm.

questions.stem: Which combination produces the shortest spatial pulse length?
options: Many cycles and a long wavelength
Many cycles and a short wavelength
Few cycles and a short wavelength
Few cycles and a long wavelength
questions.explanation: Few cycles and a short wavelength minimize SPL.

questions.stem: If the number of cycles doubles and the wavelength is unchanged, spatial pulse length:
questions.explanation: SPL = cycles × wavelength; doubling cycles doubles SPL.

questions.stem: In the same medium with a constant number of cycles, doubling the frequency causes spatial pulse length to:
questions.explanation: Doubling frequency halves wavelength and so halves SPL.

questions.stem: Which unit is appropriate for spatial pulse length?
questions.explanation: SPL is a distance (mm).

questions.stem: Spatial pulse length is determined by:
options: The number of cycles and the wavelength
questions.explanation: SPL = cycles × wavelength.

questions.stem: A 2-cycle pulse and a 3-cycle pulse both have a frequency of 5 MHz in soft tissue. Which has the shorter spatial pulse length?
questions.explanation: Same wavelength, fewer cycles gives a shorter SPL.

questions.stem: Which pulse characteristic gives the best axial resolution?
questions.explanation: A short SPL gives the best axial resolution.

questions.stem: Axial resolution equals:
questions.explanation: Axial resolution = SPL ÷ 2.

questions.stem: A pulse has a spatial pulse length of 1.2 mm. What is the axial resolution?
A pulse has a spatial pulse length of 3 mm. What is the axial resolution?
The axial resolution is 0.4 mm. What is the spatial pulse length?
Two reflectors lie very close together along the beam direction. Which change would most improve their separate display?
questions.explanation: Decreasing SPL improves axial resolution.

questions.stem: A transducer uses fewer cycles per pulse at an unchanged frequency. What is expected?
options: Longer pulse duration and poorer axial resolution
Shorter pulse duration and improved axial resolution
questions.explanation: Fewer cycles shorten PD and SPL, improving axial resolution.

questions.stem: Improved axial resolution means the system is better able to:
options: Separate reflectors lying along the beam axis
questions.explanation: Axial resolution separates reflectors along the beam axis.

questions.stem: The axial resolution is 0.6 mm. Two reflectors 0.4 mm apart along the beam will:
questions.explanation: Spacing (0.4 mm) is less than axial resolution (0.6 mm), so the echoes merge.

questions.stem: The axial resolution is 0.3 mm. Two reflectors 0.5 mm apart along the beam will:
options: Appear as a single brighter echo
questions.explanation: Spacing (0.5 mm) exceeds axial resolution (0.3 mm), so they are separate.

questions.stem: The PRP is 200 µs. What is the PRF?
The PRP is 100 µs. What is the PRF?
The PRP is 500 µs. What is the PRF?
The PRP is 250 µs. What is the PRF?
The PRF is 10 kHz. What is the PRP?
The PRF is 4 kHz. What is the PRP?
The PRF is 2 kHz. What is the PRP?
What happens to PRF when PRP increases?
questions.explanation: PRF and PRP are reciprocal.

questions.stem: If PRF doubles, PRP:
questions.explanation: Doubling PRF halves PRP.

questions.stem: Greater imaging depth requires:
questions.explanation: Deeper imaging needs longer listening time.

questions.stem: Which pulse parameter is directly related to imaging depth?
questions.explanation: Pulse repetition period is directly related to depth.

questions.stem: For a 10 cm imaging depth in soft tissue (13 µs per cm round trip), the minimum PRP needed to listen for the deepest echo is about:
questions.explanation: 10 cm × 13 µs/cm = 130 µs.

questions.stem: For a 5 cm imaging depth in soft tissue (13 µs per cm round trip), the minimum PRP is about:
questions.explanation: 5 cm × 13 µs/cm = 65 µs.

questions.stem: A 130 µs PRP corresponds to a PRF of about:
A sonographer decreases imaging depth with all other settings unchanged. What is expected?
questions.explanation: Less depth means shorter PRP and higher PRF.

questions.stem: Which unit is commonly used for PRF?
questions.explanation: PRF is commonly given in kHz.

questions.stem: Duty factor is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Duty factor = pulse duration ÷ PRP.

questions.stem: The pulse duration is 2 µs and the PRP is 400 µs. What is the duty factor?
The pulse duration is 1 µs and the PRP is 500 µs. What is the duty factor?
The pulse duration is 3 µs and the PRP is 300 µs. What is the duty factor?
The pulse duration is 0.5 µs and the PRP is 100 µs. What is the duty factor?
The pulse duration is 2 µs and the PRP is 100 µs. What is the duty factor?
The pulse duration is 1.5 µs and the PRP is 150 µs. What is the duty factor?
A duty factor of 0.005 is equal to:
Which statement about the units of duty factor is correct?
options: It is unitless (a ratio or percentage)
questions.explanation: Duty factor is a ratio or percentage with no units.

questions.stem: With pulse duration constant, increasing PRP causes duty factor to:
questions.explanation: A larger PRP makes PD ÷ PRP smaller.

questions.stem: With pulse duration constant, decreasing PRP causes duty factor to:
questions.explanation: A smaller PRP makes PD ÷ PRP larger.

questions.stem: With PRP constant, increasing pulse duration causes duty factor to:
questions.explanation: Longer pulses with the same PRP raise the ratio.

questions.stem: Which change increases duty factor when pulse duration is constant?
questions.explanation: Less depth shortens PRP, raising duty factor.

questions.stem: What happens to duty factor when imaging depth increases (pulse duration constant)?
questions.explanation: Greater depth lengthens PRP and lowers PD ÷ PRP.

questions.stem: The duty factor of a continuous wave system is:
questions.explanation: Continuous wave is always transmitting: DF = 1 (100%).

questions.stem: A pulse lasts 1 µs and the PRF is 5 kHz. What is the duty factor?
A sonographer increases the imaging depth. Which change occurs?
questions.explanation: Greater depth needs more listening time.

questions.stem: Which combination is expected when imaging depth increases?
options: PRP decreases, PRF increases, duty factor increases
PRP increases, PRF decreases, duty factor decreases
PRP increases, PRF increases, duty factor decreases
PRP decreases, PRF decreases, duty factor increases
questions.explanation: Greater depth: PRP up, PRF down, DF down.

questions.stem: Which combination is expected when imaging depth decreases?
options: PRP decreases, PRF increases, duty factor increases
PRP increases, PRF decreases, duty factor decreases
PRP increases, PRF increases, duty factor increases
PRP decreases, PRF decreases, duty factor decreases
questions.explanation: Less depth: PRP down, PRF up, DF up.

questions.stem: Which parameter is not affected by a change in imaging depth?
questions.explanation: Pulse duration does not depend on depth.

questions.stem: Which parameter is unaffected by imaging depth?
questions.explanation: SPL does not depend on depth.

questions.stem: A sonographer leaves the depth unnecessarily deep when imaging a superficial structure. The most likely consequence is:
options: Higher PRF and improved temporal resolution
Shorter PRP and increased duty factor
Shorter SPL and improved axial resolution
Lower PRF and reduced frame rate
questions.explanation: Excess depth lowers PRF and can reduce frame rate.

questions.stem: Which parameter can be changed most directly by adjusting imaging depth?
questions.explanation: Depth changes listening time, PRP and therefore PRF.

questions.stem: Which statement about duty factor and depth is correct?
options: Duty factor increases with depth because PRP increases
Duty factor decreases with depth because PRP increases
Duty factor is unchanged by depth
Duty factor increases with depth because PRF decreases
questions.explanation: Longer PRP with constant PD lowers duty factor.

questions.stem: If imaging depth doubles, PRP (dominated by listening time) approximately:
questions.explanation: Twice the depth needs about twice the listening time.

questions.stem: If imaging depth doubles, PRF approximately:
questions.explanation: PRF = 1 ÷ PRP, so it roughly halves.

questions.stem: If imaging depth is halved with pulse duration constant, duty factor approximately:
questions.explanation: PRP roughly halves, so PD ÷ PRP roughly doubles.

questions.stem: Why can PRF increase when imaging depth decreases?
options: Echoes return sooner, so less listening time is needed
More cycles are used per pulse
questions.explanation: Shallower echoes return sooner.

questions.stem: Which parameter is measured in millimetres?
questions.explanation: Spatial pulse length is a distance.

questions.stem: Which parameter is commonly expressed in kilohertz?
questions.explanation: PRF is a frequency, often in kHz.

questions.stem: Which units are appropriate for pulse repetition period?
questions.explanation: PRP is a time, in µs or ms.

questions.stem: A transducer uses fewer cycles per pulse at an unchanged frequency. The result is:
options: Longer pulse duration and poorer axial resolution
Shorter pulse duration and improved axial resolution
questions.explanation: Fewer cycles shorten PD and SPL, improving axial resolution.

questions.stem: The PRP is 0.5 ms. What is the PRF?
A pulse lasts 2 µs and the PRP is 0.4 ms. What is the duty factor?
Ultrasound can be produced in which two basic ways?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound is produced as continuous wave (CW) or pulsed wave (PW).

questions.stem: Pulsed ultrasound alternates between:
questions.explanation: Pulsed ultrasound alternates transmit (on) and receive (off) periods.

questions.stem: In pulsed ultrasound, the "on time" is when the system:
questions.explanation: On time is when the system transmits a pulse.

questions.stem: In pulsed ultrasound, the "off time" is when the system:
questions.explanation: Off time is when the system listens for returning echoes.

questions.stem: Continuous-wave ultrasound:
questions.explanation: CW ultrasound transmits continuously with no gaps.

questions.stem: Pulsed ultrasound is required for 2D imaging because it:
options: Provides measurable echo-return time for depth (range) information
questions.explanation: Pulses give a measurable echo-return time, which allows depth to be calculated.

questions.stem: Continuous wave cannot produce range-resolved B-mode imaging because it lacks a:
questions.explanation: CW has no pulse-timing reference, so it cannot create range-resolved B-mode images.

questions.stem: Multiple scan lines, each from a pulse, form a:
questions.explanation: Many scan lines together form a 2D image.

questions.stem: Ranging is also known as:
questions.explanation: Ranging is also called echo location.

questions.stem: Every echo displayed on the screen represents sound that:
options: Travelled to a reflector and back to the transducer (round trip)
questions.explanation: Each displayed echo left the transducer, reflected from a structure, and returned (round trip).

questions.stem: The round-trip travel time of ultrasound in soft tissue is about:
questions.explanation: About 13 µs of round-trip time is needed for every centimetre of depth.

questions.stem: The speed of sound assumed by ultrasound systems in soft tissue is:
questions.explanation: Systems assume 1540 m/s in soft tissue.

questions.stem: The range equation is:
questions.explanation: Range = (c × t) ÷ 2.

questions.stem: The echo travel time is divided by two because:
options: The echo travels to the reflector and back, so only half the time is the one-way distance
questions.explanation: The measured time covers the trip to the reflector and back, so it is divided by two.

questions.stem: An echo returns 26 µs after the pulse. The reflector depth is:
questions.explanation: 26 µs ÷ 13 µs/cm = 2 cm.

questions.stem: An echo returns 65 µs after the pulse. The reflector depth is:
The round-trip time for a reflector at 8 cm is:
questions.explanation: 8 cm × 13 µs/cm = 104 µs.

questions.stem: An echo returns after 39 µs. The depth is:
Which list contains the five parameters of pulsed sound?
questions.explanation: The five parameters are PD, SPL, PRP, PRF and DF.

questions.stem: Cycles grouped together with gaps between them form:
questions.explanation: Cycles grouped with gaps between groups form pulsed ultrasound.

questions.stem: The gap between pulses is the:
questions.explanation: The gap between pulses is the off time, when echoes are received.

questions.stem: Pulse duration (PD) is:
options: The time between the start of one pulse and the next
The number of pulses per second
The time for a pulse to occur
questions.explanation: PD is the time for a pulse to occur (on time only).

questions.stem: The unit of pulse duration is:
questions.explanation: PD is measured in microseconds.

questions.stem: Pulse duration includes:
questions.explanation: PD represents transmit time only and does not include receive time.

questions.stem: Pulse duration is calculated as:
questions.explanation: PD = number of cycles × period.

questions.stem: If the period increases while the number of cycles stays the same, pulse duration:
questions.explanation: A longer period means a longer PD for the same number of cycles.

questions.stem: If the number of cycles per pulse increases at the same frequency, pulse duration:
questions.explanation: More cycles per pulse means a longer PD.

questions.stem: A pulse has 4 cycles at 2 MHz. The pulse duration is:
A pulse has 3 cycles at 5 MHz. The pulse duration is:
Two pulses both have 5 cycles, one at 5 MHz and one at 10 MHz. The 10 MHz pulse duration is:
options: Half that of the 5 MHz pulse
Double that of the 5 MHz pulse
The same as the 5 MHz pulse
questions.explanation: 5 MHz: PD = 5 × 0.2 = 1 µs. 10 MHz: PD = 5 × 0.1 = 0.5 µs, which is half.

questions.stem: B-mode imaging typically uses pulses of about:
questions.explanation: B-mode uses very short pulses of about 2–3 cycles.

questions.stem: Doppler pulses are typically:
questions.explanation: Doppler uses longer pulses of about 5–30 cycles.

questions.stem: Continuous wave Doppler is characterised by:
options: No pulsing; the signal is on continuously
questions.explanation: CW Doppler has no pulsing; the signal is on continuously.

questions.stem: Is pulse duration directly adjustable by the sonographer?
questions.explanation: PD is not directly adjustable by the sonographer.

questions.stem: Pulse duration depends on:
questions.explanation: PD depends on cycles per pulse and the period.

questions.stem: The period of a pulse is determined by the:
questions.explanation: Period is determined by the operating frequency.

questions.stem: Changing the operating frequency can:
options: Not affect pulse duration at all
questions.explanation: Changing frequency changes the period, so it indirectly changes PD.

questions.stem: A shorter pulse duration improves:
questions.explanation: Shorter PD supports better axial resolution.

questions.stem: If cycles per pulse stay the same and frequency increases, pulse duration:
questions.explanation: A higher frequency shortens the period, so PD decreases when the cycle count is unchanged.

questions.stem: A shorter pulse duration reduces:
questions.explanation: A shorter PD reduces echo overlap, which improves axial resolution.

questions.stem: Spatial pulse length (SPL) is:
options: The length of space occupied by one pulse
The number of pulses per second
questions.explanation: SPL is the length of space occupied by one pulse.

questions.stem: SPL is calculated as:
questions.explanation: SPL = wavelength × number of cycles.

questions.stem: A common unit for SPL in diagnostic ultrasound is the:
questions.explanation: SPL is a length, commonly in millimetres.

questions.stem: A pulse of 4 cycles at 2 MHz in soft tissue (λ = 0.77 mm) has an SPL of:
A pulse of 3 cycles with a wavelength of 0.5 mm has an SPL of:
A longer wavelength gives a:
questions.explanation: Longer wavelength means longer SPL.

questions.stem: Fewer cycles per pulse give a:
questions.explanation: Fewer cycles per pulse means shorter SPL.

questions.stem: If cycles per pulse remain unchanged, a higher frequency:
questions.explanation: A higher frequency shortens wavelength, so SPL shortens when cycles are unchanged.

questions.stem: Is SPL directly adjustable by the sonographer?
questions.explanation: SPL is not directly adjustable.

questions.stem: A shorter SPL improves:
questions.explanation: Shorter SPL improves axial resolution.

questions.stem: Which two pulsed parameters do NOT depend on imaging depth?
questions.explanation: PD and SPL depend on the source (cycles, frequency, medium), not on depth.

questions.stem: Which three pulsed parameters change with imaging depth?
questions.explanation: PRP, PRF and DF change with imaging depth.

questions.stem: Pulse repetition period (PRP) is the time:
options: From the start of one pulse to the start of the next
Occupied by the off time only
questions.explanation: PRP is measured from the start of one pulse to the start of the next.

questions.stem: PRP includes:
questions.explanation: PRP = transmit (on) time + receive (off) time.

questions.stem: PRP is measured in:
questions.explanation: PRP is measured in microseconds or milliseconds.

questions.stem: Greater imaging depth produces a:
questions.explanation: Greater depth needs more listening time, so PRP is longer.

questions.stem: The PRP for an imaging depth of 10 cm is about:
questions.explanation: 10 cm × 13 µs/cm = 130 µs.

questions.stem: The PRP for an imaging depth of 4 cm is about:
The minimum PRP must allow:
options: Echoes from the deepest reflector to return
questions.explanation: PRP must be long enough for echoes from the deepest reflector to return before the next pulse.

questions.stem: PRP and PRF describe:
questions.explanation: PRP and PRF describe the timing between pulses.

questions.stem: Period and frequency describe:
questions.explanation: Period and frequency describe a single wave (cycle). They are different from PRP and PRF.

questions.stem: Pulse repetition frequency (PRF) is the number of:
questions.explanation: PRF is the number of pulses transmitted each second.

questions.stem: PRF is measured in:
questions.explanation: PRF is measured in Hz or kHz.

questions.stem: The typical PRF range in clinical imaging is about:
questions.explanation: Typical clinical imaging PRF is 1–10 kHz.

questions.stem: PRF is the ______ of PRP.
questions.explanation: PRF = 1/PRP.

questions.stem: A PRP of 250 µs corresponds to a PRF of:
A PRF of 5 kHz corresponds to a PRP of:
When imaging depth increases, PRF:
questions.explanation: PRF is inversely related to imaging depth.

questions.stem: A shallower imaging depth gives a:
questions.explanation: Shallower depth means shorter PRP and higher PRF.

questions.stem: At a depth of 10 cm, PRP is 130 µs, so PRF is approximately:
At a depth of 5 cm, PRP is 65 µs, so PRF is approximately:
PRF is determined by:
questions.explanation: PRF is determined by propagation velocity and imaging depth.

questions.stem: One single pulse corresponds to:
options: One scan line on the display
questions.explanation: One pulse produces one scan line of image information.

questions.stem: To maximise PRF, a sonographer should:
options: Use the shallowest depth that includes the anatomy of interest
questions.explanation: The shallowest useful depth maximises PRF, which improves frame rate and temporal resolution.

questions.stem: A higher PRF can support a:
options: Higher frame rate and better temporal resolution
questions.explanation: Higher PRF supports a higher frame rate and better temporal resolution.

questions.stem: Duty factor (DF) is the:
options: Fraction (percentage) of time the system transmits
Fraction of time the system receives
questions.explanation: Duty factor is the percentage of time the system is transmitting.

questions.stem: Which formula gives duty factor?
questions.explanation: DF = (PD / PRP) × 100.

questions.stem: Duty factor is usually expressed as a:
questions.explanation: DF is expressed as a percentage.

questions.stem: A pulse with PD = 2 µs and PRP = 200 µs has a duty factor of:
A pulse with PD = 1 µs and PRP = 250 µs has a duty factor of:
If pulse duration increases and PRP stays the same, duty factor:
questions.explanation: PD and DF move in the same direction.

questions.stem: If PRP increases and PD stays the same, duty factor:
questions.explanation: PRP and DF move in opposite directions.

questions.stem: Greater imaging depth produces a:
questions.explanation: Greater depth means longer PRP and therefore lower DF.

questions.stem: Shallower imaging depth gives a:
questions.explanation: Shallower depth means shorter PRP and therefore higher DF.

questions.stem: The duty factor of continuous-wave ultrasound is:
questions.explanation: CW is always transmitting, so DF = 100%.

questions.stem: The sonographer changes duty factor:
questions.explanation: PD is not adjusted directly, so DF changes indirectly through depth (PRP).

questions.stem: If the imaging depth is doubled, PRF is:
questions.explanation: Depth doubles, so PRP doubles and PRF is halved.

questions.stem: If the imaging depth is doubled (PD constant), duty factor is:
questions.explanation: Depth doubles, so PRP doubles; with PD constant, DF is halved.

questions.stem: Frame rate is:
options: The time to create one frame
The number of frames per second
The number of pulses per frame
The number of cycles per pulse
questions.explanation: Frame rate is the number of frames per second.

questions.stem: Frame time is:
options: The number of frames per second
The time required to create one complete frame
questions.explanation: Frame time is the time needed to create one complete frame.

questions.stem: Frame rate and frame time are:
questions.explanation: Frame rate = 1 / frame time.

questions.stem: A frame time of 50 ms gives a frame rate of:
A frame rate of 40 Hz gives a frame time of:
If imaging depth increases (with the same number of scan lines), frame rate:
questions.explanation: Greater depth lowers PRF, so frames take longer to build and frame rate falls.

questions.stem: Scanned modalities:
options: Sweep the ultrasound beam across a region to build an image
Transmit in the same direction repeatedly
questions.explanation: Scanned modalities sweep the beam across a region to build an image.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a scanned modality?
questions.explanation: B-mode is a scanned modality. M-mode, A-mode and CW Doppler are non-scanned.

questions.stem: Non-scanned modalities:
options: Sweep the beam across a wide field
Transmit the acoustic beam in the same direction repeatedly
questions.explanation: Non-scanned modalities transmit the beam in the same direction repeatedly.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a non-scanned modality?
questions.explanation: M-mode is non-scanned (like A-mode, CW Doppler and single-gate PW Doppler).

questions.stem: Compared with scanned modalities, non-scanned modalities present:
questions.explanation: Non-scanned modalities present greater thermal risks than scanned modalities.

questions.stem: In colour Doppler, multiple acoustic lines sent along one direction are generally called a:
questions.explanation: Colour Doppler sends multiple acoustic lines per colour display line, called a colour packet.
